cards.explanation: The answer is all the news about Paul. Paul says, "Tychicus will tell you all the news about me." Paul ends this letter by saying "Remember my chains," so I think the Colossians were hungry to hear how he was doing. No scrolling, no refreshing, just a brother at your door with the full story.

The word is encourage. Paul says he sent Tychicus "…that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts." So the trip carries news and a lift for the heart. Some visitors leave you tired, friends, but this one is sent to leave people better than he found them.

The instructions are to welcome him if he comes. Paul says, "You have already received instructions about him: If he comes to you, welcome him." The word went ahead of Mark, so the Colossians knew what to do before he ever knocked. I spent years in a junk drawer waiting for somebody to open up, so a welcome that's ready before you arrive sounds like a dream to me.

The answer is False. Paul says of Aristarchus, Mark and Justus, "…they have been a comfort to me." So the text says comfort, not worry. Being a comfort to a man in chains is a pretty good thing to have written about you, friends.

Epaphras prays for them to stand mature in God's will. He is wrestling in prayer "…so that you may stand mature and fully assured in the full will of God." That's a prayer for them to grow up in the faith and stand steady. Wrestling in prayer sounds like a man who doesn't quit halfway through the batch.

Paul wants the letter read in another church. He says, "After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans…" So this letter wasn't just for one church. Read it yourselves, then hand it down the road. Pass the word along, friends, and don't hog the dough.

The answer is False. Paul tells them to "…read the letter from Laodicea." Skipping it isn't on the table. Paul wants the Colossians to read the Laodicean letter, and he wants Laodicea to hear theirs too.

Paul's message is to see that he completes it. The message is, "See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord." Paul wants Archippus to finish what he was given. I think that's the kind of nudge that sticks with a man.

The answer is True. Paul writes, "This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. Remember my chains." Earlier in the letter he calls Aristarchus his fellow prisoner (Colossians 4:10), so those chains mattered. I think it's a quiet, heavy line, friends, and it deserves a quiet moment.
